Field surveys conducted along the middle basin of the Magdalena River have provided detailed morphometric data for Prochilodus magdalenae. Adult individuals sampled during the ascending reproductive migration exhibited a maximum recorded total length of 51 centimeters [Li = 51 centimeters], a size that positions this species as one of the larger-bodied members within the Prochilodontidae family. The population structure revealed that sexual maturation typically coincides with the attainment of a total length of 24.5 centimeters [Lp = 24.5 centimeters], marking a clear ontogenetic threshold for the onset of gonadal development. Specimens below this length were invariably classified as immature, confirming a discrete size-based transition to reproductive capability. Body mass at the pubertal stage averaged 241 grams [Wwp = 241 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required before reproductive tissues begin to differentiate. These morphometric benchmarks were consistent across multiple sampling years and hydrological regimes, suggesting a stable life-history strategy that is finely tuned to the seasonal flood pulse dynamics of the river system. The largest gravid females in the sample reached an ultimate wet weight of 2110 grams [Wwi = 2110 grams], a value that underscores considerable post-pubertal growth and the ability to accumulate significant lipid reserves for gametogenesis and spawning migrations.

The early life stages of Prochilodus magdalenae are characterized by rapid development under the thermal conditions of the Magdalena floodplain. Eggs incubated at a stable water temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C] undergo embryonic development and hatch after approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], a relatively brief incubation period typical of potamodromous characiform species that spawn in warm, productive environments. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still completely dependent on its endogenous reserves, has a minimal wet weight at birth of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of roughly 0.8 millimeters from which it hatches. This diminutive size at the onset of the lecithotrophic phase places the prolarvae among the most vulnerable life stages, subject to high mortality from predation and starvation before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. The rapid yolk absorption and the transition to first feeding must occur within a narrow temporal window, underscoring the critical nature of the hatchling interval in determining recruitment success in the lowland river environment.

Lifespan estimates for Magdalena River prochilodus, derived from scale annuli analysis and length-frequency distributions of multiple cohorts, indicate a maximum longevity extending to 10 years [am = 10 years] under the prevailing thermal regime of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]. This lifespan, which translates to approximately 3650 days from the moment of hatching, is consistent with the iteroparous life history observed in other large-bodied migratory characiforms of South America. The species exhibits a slow senescence pattern, with adults maintaining reproductive condition well into their later years. Growth asymptotes are approached gradually; the ultimate total length of 51 centimeters [Li = 51 centimeters] is typically reached between the seventh and eighth year of life, after which somatic expansion slows markedly. The ultimate wet weight, recorded at 2110 grams [Wwi = 2110 grams], represents the maximum body mass achievable under optimal foraging conditions in floodplain habitats, though most individuals in the population attain a slightly lower asymptotic size. The longevity data suggest that the species can withstand several annual migratory cycles and repeated spawning events across its decade-long reproductive window.

Reproductive output in Prochilodus magdalenae has been quantified through direct ovarian examination and volumetric estimation of oocyte batches. Gravid females are highly fecund, producing on average 85,000 oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = 85,000 oocytes per spawning event], a value that reflects the large body cavity capacity and the extensive ovarian investment characteristic of migratory characids. The spawning frequency is limited by the annual hydrological cycle, with most individuals undertaking a single spawning migration each year [F_R_i = single spawning migration each year] during the rising water phase of the Magdalena River. This annual reproductive bout is synchronized with the flood pulse that inundates the floodplain, providing nursery habitats rich in zooplankton for the exogenously feeding larvae. The combination of high fecundity and restricted annual spawning represents a bet-hedging strategy that optimizes offspring survival during the brief period of peak floodplain productivity. The attainment of puberty at 24.5 centimeters [Lp = 24.5 centimeters] total length ensures that individuals have reached a body size adequate to support the large oocyte complement required for a successful single annual spawn.

Comparative physiological analysis of Prochilodus magdalenae reveals interesting life-history tradeoffs when contextualized among its South American congeners. The wet weight at puberty of 241 grams [Wwp = 241 grams] represents approximately eleven percent of the ultimate wet weight of 2110 grams [Wwi = 2110 grams], indicating that the species delays reproductive onset until a considerable fraction of asymptotic mass is achieved. This pattern contrasts with smaller-bodied prochilodontids that mature at a higher relative mass, suggesting an adaptive response to the risks and energetic demands of long-distance upstream migration. The total length at puberty of 24.5 centimeters [Lp = 24.5 centimeters] is almost exactly half of the ultimate total length of 51 centimeters [Li = 51 centimeters], a metric that aligns with the general teleost pattern of maturation at roughly fifty percent of maximum size. The age at birth of 5 days [ab = 5 days] at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C] and the maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] at the same temperature define a compressed early development phase balanced against an extended adult reproductive tenure, a life-history syndrome well suited to seasonally predictable environments where spawning windows and larval rearing conditions are tightly coupled to the annual flood regime.
